title: Section 123 — Causing hurt by means of poison, etc., with intent to commit an offence

content.overview: BNS s. 123 — Causing hurt by means of poison, etc., with intent to commit an offence.
content.study:
Introduction and meaning
Causing hurt by means of poison, etc., with intent to commit an offence. BNS restatement of IPC 328. Elements are substantially the same; cite the BNS number for offences on or after 1 July 2024. BNS restatement of IPC 328. Cite the BNS number for facts on or after 1 July 2024.
In student language: BNS s. 123 is the rule on “Causing hurt by means of poison, etc., with intent to commit an offence”. The section provides that whoever administers to or causes to be taken by any person any poison or any stupefying, intoxicating or unwholesome drug, or other thing with intent to cause hurt to such person, or with intent to commit or to facilitate the commission of an offence or knowing it to be likely that he will thereby cause hurt, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 123 exists so that “Causing hurt by means of poison, etc., with intent to commit an offence” has a closed legal test in Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: Homicide, organised crime, terrorism, hurt, acid, restraint, assault, kidnapping and trafficking.

learningObjectives: Master the elements of administering poison, stupefying, intoxicating, or unwholesome drugs under BNS s. 123.
Analyze the specific mens rea: intent to commit or facilitate an offence, or knowing it likely that an offence will be committed.
Examine the ten-year imprisonment tier and fine.
Understand the application to drink-spiking, date-rape drugs, and robbery facilitation.
enhancement.definition: BNS s. 123 penalizes whoever administers to or causes to be taken by any person any poison or any stupefying, intoxicating or unwholesome drug, or other thing with intent to cause hurt to such person, or with intent to commit or to facilitate the commission of an offence, or knowing it to be likely that he will thereby cause hurt, with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Criminalizes the surreptitious chemical incapacitation of victims through poison, sedatives, or intoxicants aimed at facilitating felonies such as theft, robbery, or sexual assault.
statutoryFramework: Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body, BNS s. 123 (corresponding to IPC s. 328).
Substances covered: Poison, stupefying drug, intoxicating drug, unwholesome drug, or any other noxious thing.
Actus reus: Administering to, or causing to be taken by, any person.
Mens rea: Intent to cause hurt, OR intent to commit/facilitate an offence, OR knowledge that hurt is likely.
Punishment: Imprisonment of either description extending up to ten years, and fine.
essentialIngredients: The substance administered was a poison, stupefying drug, intoxicating drug, unwholesome drug, or other noxious thing.
The accused administered the substance to the victim, or caused the victim to take it.
The act was done with intent to cause hurt; OR with intent to commit or facilitate the commission of an offence; OR with knowledge that hurt was likely.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 123 carries forward Section 328 of the IPC, targeting treacherous chemical attacks. The provision is widely invoked in cases of drink-spiking on public transport (where travelers are drugged to steal luggage), chemical incapacitation in hotels, and the administration of date-rape drugs (such as benzodiazepines, ketamine, or chloral hydrate) to facilitate sexual assault. The phrase 'stupefying, intoxicating or unwholesome drug' is construed broadly to cover any substance that dulls the senses, produces drowsiness, impairs judgment, or produces gastrointestinal illness. The offence is complete upon the administration with the requisite intent, even if the intended secondary crime (such as theft or rape) is interrupted or fails.
examples: Teaching example (Drugging train passenger for theft): An accused offers a fellow train passenger a cup of tea covertly laced with heavy sleeping pills, intending to render the passenger unconscious to steal his laptop bag. Once the victim drinks the tea, the offence under s. 123 is complete (punishable with up to 10 years).

Teaching example (Drink-spiking before sexual assault): An accused slips a colorless, odorless sedative into a woman's cocktail at a lounge with the intention of facilitating sexual relations while she is incapacitated. The accused is liable under s. 123 (and s. 63 if sexual acts ensue).
distinctions: Section 123 vs Simple Hurt (s. 115): Simple hurt carries 1 year; Section 123 imposes an aggravated 10-year penalty because poison/drugs are insidious weapons used to facilitate crimes.

Section 123 vs Attempt to Murder (s. 109): If the poison is administered in a lethal dose with intention to kill, the offence is attempt to murder; Section 123 applies where the substance is administered to cause hurt, stupefy, or facilitate a crime.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether an accused who mixed eye drops (tetrahydrozoline) into a colleague's beverage to cause severe nausea and diarrhea so the colleague would miss a job interview is guilty under s. 123.
Rule: Administering an unwholesome drug or thing with intent to cause hurt satisfies BNS s. 123.
Application: Eye drops consumed orally act as an unwholesome chemical causing physiological infirmity (hurt), administered intentionally.
Conclusion: The accused is guilty of an offence under BNS s. 123.

keyTakeaways: Criminalizes administering poison, sedatives, intoxicants, or unwholesome drugs.
Targets chemical incapacitation to facilitate crimes like robbery or sexual assault.
Completed upon administration with intent; success of secondary crime is not required.
Punishable with imprisonment up to ten years and fine.
